screens.title: Configuring Routing Policies — Actions
screens.subtitle: How Junos 'then' statements change a route's fate and attributes

narration.text: In this chapter we explore the Junos 'then' actions: the explicit decisions and attribute changes you apply to matched routes. You will learn the basic accept and reject controls, flow-control verbs that change evaluation order, and the attribute modifiers used most often in BGP for traffic engineering. Understanding these actions is essential because they determine whether a route is installed, how it appears to peers, and how traffic flows into and out of your network. For example, local-preference influences which exit your AS uses for outbound traffic, while as-path-prepend makes your advertised routes less attractive to peers. We will also highlight common pitfalls: forgetting a final accept after a next-term or using community set when you intended to append. Throughout the lesson you will see concrete Junos configuration examples and a short hands-on lab that walks through creating a community, applying a policy, and verifying the changes. By the end you'll be able to choose the right action to accept, reject, or transform a route and reason about the operational effect before you commit it.

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Routing policy actions let you control acceptance, evaluation flow, and BGP attributes so you can safely influence path selection and advertisement behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives describe measurable skills you will gain. First, you will implement standard routing policy actions such as accept and reject. That means you will confidently decide whether a route is installed or dropped, and you will understand implicit fall-through behavior when no accept or reject is present. Second, you will use flow control actions — specifically next-term and next-policy — to shape policy evaluation. You will understand when to continue evaluation inside the same policy versus handing the route to another policy. Third, you will modify common BGP attributes like metric, local-preference, community, and as-path-prepend to influence how peers and your own AS choose paths. You will know which attributes are protocol specific. Fourth, you will configure install-nexthop for targeted forwarding changes and understand its impact on the forwarding plane. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can show evidence of competency by reading route output or showing attribute values in the route details.

keyIdea.title: Verified outcomes

screens.title: Accept and Reject — explicit route fate
screens.subtitle: How explicit decisions determine installation and implicit fall-through behaviour

narration.text: When a route matches a term, the most fundamental decisions are accept and reject. An accept action allows the route to be processed by the routing protocol and potentially installed in the routing table. A reject action discards the route entirely, preventing the route from being used or advertised further. One operational detail to remember is implicit behavior: if a term matches but contains no explicit accept or reject, evaluation continues to the next term; if evaluation reaches the end of the policy statement without an accept, the route is implicitly rejected. This implicit rejection is a frequent source of confusion because a route that matched a term may still disappear if no explicit accept is encountered later. A concrete example is a policy that sets a community in term one and uses next-term to continue evaluation; if no later term accepts the route, that route is ultimately rejected even though earlier actions modified it. A common misconception is to assume that a set of attribute modifications alone will cause installation; modifications only alter attributes — you still need accept to install. Key takeaway: always include an explicit accept or a controlled chain of policies that guarantees acceptance when you intend for the route to be used.

keyIdea.title: Core claim
keyIdea.text: Accept installs a route; reject discards it. Attribute changes do not install a route by themselves—an accept is still required.

content.html:
Core Concept
Accept and Reject
Explicitly decide whether a matched route is installed or discarded. Implicit rejection occurs if no accept is found by the end of the policy.
Explanation
  • accept allows protocol processing and potential installation.
  • reject prevents use and advertisement of the route.
  • Matching without accept causes fall-through; reaching policy end implicitly rejects.
Concrete example
A term that only sets a community but does not accept will not install the route unless a later term accepts it.
Key Takeaway

Always pair attribute changes with an accept later in the policy, or ensure an applied policy chain will accept the route.

Junos example
set policy-options policy-statement EXAMPLE term T1 from prefix-list 203.0.113.0/24
set policy-options policy-statement EXAMPLE term T1 then community add NO_EXPORT
set policy-options policy-statement EXAMPLE term T1 then next-term

set policy-options policy-statement EXAMPLE term T2 then accept
Here T1 modifies a route then continues. T2 accepts it; without T2 the route is implicitly rejected.
Common mistake
Assuming that setting a community will install the route. Attribute changes do not substitute for accept.

screens.title: Flow Control — next-term and next-policy
screens.subtitle: How policy evaluation moves between terms and policies

narration.text: Flow control actions change the path of policy evaluation. next-term instructs Junos to stop processing the current term and immediately evaluate the next term within the same policy statement. This is useful when you want to apply one set of actions — such as adding a community — and then allow subsequent terms to further match or finally accept or reject the route. next-policy stops processing the current policy statement entirely and hands the route to the next policy in the applied chain. This is commonly used when you have multiple policies applied in order, and you want a matched route in the first policy to be evaluated by a second policy for different checks or final acceptance. A common operational pitfall is forgetting that next-term or next-policy do not implicitly accept the route. If you next-term into a sequence that never accepts, the route will ultimately be implicitly rejected. Another gotcha is assuming next-policy merges actions; it transfers control — actions applied before next-policy remain, but acceptance must still occur later. A practical example: add a community with next-term, then a later term sets local-preference and accepts. Testing in a lab ensures your sequencing yields the intended installed attributes. What question should you ask before using next-policy? Know exactly which policy will run next and whether it will accept.

keyIdea.title: Control insight
keyIdea.text: Use next-term to continue inside a policy and next-policy to hand off to the next applied policy; both require eventual accept to install the route.

content.html:
Process Flow
next-term vs next-policy
Decide whether the evaluation continues inside the same policy or moves to the next policy in a chain.
Step sequence
  1. Term matches and applies actions before flow control.
  2. If next-term, evaluation resumes at the next term in the same policy.
  3. If next-policy, evaluation continues at the first term of the next applied policy.
  4. At some point a term must accept or the route is implicitly rejected.
Pro Tip

Map the policy chain before using next-policy. Know which policy follows and whether it will accept the route.

Concrete example
set policy-options policy-statement CHAIN term SET_COMM then community add ISP_TAG
set policy-options policy-statement CHAIN term SET_COMM then next-term
set policy-options policy-statement CHAIN term FINAL then local-preference 200
set policy-options policy-statement CHAIN term FINAL then accept

# Or chain policies:
set policy-options policy-statement POLICY_A term T1 then community add A_TAG
set policy-options policy-statement POLICY_A term T1 then next-policy
set policy-options policy-statement POLICY_B term B1 then accept
In the first example the community is added, then the next term sets local-preference and accepts. In the second, POLICY_A hands the route to POLICY_B for final decision.
Common mistake: forgetting to accept after next-term/next-policy, causing implicit rejection.

screens.title: Attribute Modification — protocol context
screens.subtitle: Which attributes apply to which routing protocols and why it matters

narration.text: Routing policy actions include powerful attribute modification capabilities, but these actions are meaningful only in the proper protocol context. For example, local-preference and as-path-prepend are BGP-specific: local-preference influences how your AS chooses an exit for outbound traffic, and as-path-prepend lengthens the AS path you advertise to make your routes less preferred by peers. Metric is a more general attribute but maps to MED in BGP; it affects how external ASes choose an entry point into your AS when MED is considered. Community tags are BGP constructs used as metadata to signal behavior to peers or later policy terms; they can be added, replaced with set, or removed with delete. Not all protocols accept all changes — attempting to set BGP-only attributes in a policy applied to OSPF routes has no meaningful effect. When designing policies, always match the attribute to the protocol and verify with route detail commands. A common misconception is that a single attribute change will have identical impact across all protocols; it will not. Understand protocol semantics to avoid surprising routing outcomes. Attribute Modification — protocol context means only apply attribute changes that make sense for the protocol; local-preference and as-path-prepend are bgp-specific, metric maps to med in bgp.. In practical terms, which attributes apply to which routing protocols and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Protocol-aware editing
keyIdea.text: Only apply attribute changes that make sense for the protocol; local-preference and as-path-prepend are BGP-specific, metric maps to MED in BGP.

content.html:
Definition
Attribute modification — protocol context
Attributes only influence routing decisions when the protocol uses them; design policies accordingly.
BGP-only
local-preference, as-path-prepend, community
General / MED
metric maps to MED in BGP; influences external AS entry when considered.
Why this matters
  • Applying the wrong attribute wastes operations and can mislead troubleshooting.
  • Protocol semantics determine which attributes influence path selection.
  • Verification must read the route detail to confirm attribute presence.
Quick reference
Use this cheat-sheet when building terms:
local-preference — BGP inbound exit choice
as-path-prepend — lengthen AS path to de-prefer advertised routes
community add/set/delete — metadata tag for routing decisions and export
Common misconception: metric always changes path preference the same way across protocols. It does not; in BGP metric means MED.

screens.title: Metric (MED) — influence external AS entry
screens.subtitle: Set MED in Junos and reason about its use

narration.text: Metric, in the Junos routing policy context, maps to BGP's MED. MED is used by external autonomous systems to choose an entry point into your AS; a lower MED is preferred. When you set metric in a policy term, you are suggesting to external neighbors which path they should prefer when multiple entry points exist. This is less authoritative than local-preference within your own AS, but it is useful for multi-homed designs. The practical Junos configuration is a single line inside a policy term that sets metric to a value such as 100. After committing, you verify the impact with show route protocol bgp detail on a peer or by asking your peer to inspect the path. A common operational subtlety: MED can be ignored or overridden by the peer's policies and BGP settings, so changes to metric may not produce immediate or global effects. Use MED for gentle steering and combine it with communities or peer-specific policies for consistent behavior. Always test MED changes in a lab and look at 'MED' fields in route detail output to confirm the value.

keyIdea.title: Practical note
keyIdea.text: Metric sets MED for BGP; it's a suggestion to peers about entry preference. Test and verify with show route protocol bgp detail.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Setting metric (MED)
A lower MED is preferred by external ASes. Use for multi-homed entry selection.
set policy-options policy-statement MODIFY_MED term T1 from protocol bgp
set policy-options policy-statement MODIFY_MED term T1 then metric 100
set policy-options policy-statement MODIFY_MED term T1 then accept
Verify with show route protocol bgp detail and look for the MED or metric field in the route attributes.
Example scenario
You operate two peering links to the same provider. Set a lower MED on the preferred peering to nudge the provider to prefer that entry point into your AS.
Misconception
Believing MED always wins: peers may ignore or reweight MED, or apply route-flap damping. MED is not as decisive as AS path length or local-preference in BGP selection.
Key Takeaway

Use metric to advise remote peers about preferred entry. Confirm with route detail and coordinate with your peer for predictable results.

screens.title: Local-preference — inbound exit control
screens.subtitle: Raise local-preference to prefer specific routes inside your AS

narration.text: Local-preference is a BGP attribute that influences how routers inside your AS choose the exit point for traffic destined to other autonomous systems. A higher local-preference is preferred. In practice, you set local-preference on routes learned from particular neighbors to ensure traffic leaves your network through a desired uplink. The Junos configuration is straightforward: inside a policy term you set local-preference to a numeric value such as 200. After committing, inspect 'show route protocol bgp detail' or the BGP neighbor's route table to see the local-preference attribute on learned routes. One typical use case is preferring a paying customer's routes or preferring a low-cost transit via local-preference. A common misconception is to confuse local-preference with MED; local-preference affects selection within your AS, while MED affects how remote ASes pick the entry to yours. Because local-preference is evaluated before AS path length in BGP decision process, raising it reliably changes the chosen path within your AS. Always test with realistic prefixes and verify that route selection aligns with expectations. Local-preference — inbound exit control means use local-preference to control which exit your as chooses for outbound traffic; higher is preferred and it's evaluated early in bgp selection.. In practical terms, raise local-preference to prefer specific routes inside your as. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Why local-pref
keyIdea.text: Use local-preference to control which exit your AS chooses for outbound traffic; higher is preferred and it's evaluated early in BGP selection.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Set local-preference
Raise the local-preference to steer inbound choice of exit from your AS.
set policy-options policy-statement SET_LOCAL_PREF term T1 from neighbor 203.0.113.1
set policy-options policy-statement SET_LOCAL_PREF term T1 then local-preference 300
set policy-options policy-statement SET_LOCAL_PREF term T1 then accept
Verify with show route protocol bgp detail and look for 'Local preference: 300' in the route details for routes learned from that neighbor.
Example scenario
If ISP A is a preferred exit for most traffic, set a higher local-preference for routes learned from ISP A to bias egress through that provider.
Misconception: local-preference changes how other ASes prefer your advertised routes. It does not. Local-pref is internal to your AS for selecting exit.
Key Takeaway

Use local-preference for internal egress control; it is a strong and reliable lever in the BGP decision process.

screens.title: Community add vs set vs delete
screens.subtitle: How to tag routes safely and a frequent pitfall

narration.text: BGP communities are arbitrary tags you attach to routes for signaling and later policy decisions. Junos supports three primary community actions: add appends a community to the existing list, set replaces all existing communities with the new one(s), and delete removes specified communities. The operational difference is critical. If you want to mark a route for downstream handling without removing other tags, use add. If you intend to overwrite all previous tags and assert exactly the communities you want, use set. A common operational mistake is using set when you intended to append; set removes all previous communities and can unintentionally strip useful metadata established by upstream peers. Use delete when you specifically want to remove a community. Example: when partnering with an ISP that expects a particular community to be preserved for later export, adding an additional tag with add is the safe approach. Always verify community lists with the route detail output and coordinate community semantics with your peers. The key question before changing communities is: will I remove upstream tags that other policies or peers rely on?

keyIdea.title: Safety rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer community add when you intend to append tags; only use set when you deliberately want to replace all existing communities.

content.html:
Comparison
community add | set | delete
Choose add to append, set to replace, delete to remove specific entries.
add — appends a new community to any existing tags.
set — replaces all existing communities with the given set.
delete — removes specified communities from the route.
Junos example
set policy-options community NO_EXPORT_COMMUNITY members "no-export"
set policy-options policy-statement ADD_COMMUNITY term T1 then community add NO_EXPORT_COMMUNITY

# To replace:
set policy-options policy-statement REPLACE_COMM term T1 then community set ISP_TAG

# To remove:
set policy-options policy-statement REMOVE_COMM term T1 then community delete OLD_TAG
Common mistake: replacing (set) when you intended to append (add), accidentally removing upstream communities needed by other policies.
Key Takeaway

When in doubt, add to preserve upstream tags. Use set only when overwriting is intentional and coordinated.

screens.title: AS path prepend — make advertised routes less preferred
screens.subtitle: Why and how to lengthen your AS path before advertising

narration.text: AS path prepend is a commonly used export action that prepends your own AS number to the AS path of routes you advertise. BGP prefers shorter AS paths, so prepending extra copies of your AS makes the route look less attractive to external peers, steering them to prefer alternative entry points. In Junos you specify the AS numbers to prepend as a string in the as-path-prepend action. For example, repeating your AS twice makes the path appear longer. Use this technique for outbound traffic engineering when you want your traffic to leave your network via another peer. Remember that excessive prepending can complicate troubleshooting and interact with route aggregation or AS path filtering. Also note that AS path prepend is effective for influencing remote decisions but does not affect selection inside your own AS — that's local-preference. Always test prepends in a controlled environment and verify the AS path seen by remote peers using show route advertising-protocol or by coordinating with your peers. AS path prepend — make advertised routes less preferred means as path prepend lengthens the advertised path to make your routes less preferred by peers — use it carefully for outbound steering.. In practical terms, why and how to lengthen your as path before advertising. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tactical use
keyIdea.text: AS path prepend lengthens the advertised path to make your routes less preferred by peers — use it carefully for outbound steering.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
as-path-prepend
Prepend your AS to make advertised routes look longer and less preferred.
set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS term T1 then as-path-prepend "65500 65500"
set policy-options policy-statement PREPEND_AS term T1 then accept
Verify what remote peers see by checking show route advertising-protocol bgp or coordinating with the peer to inspect the AS path.
Example scenario
You prefer ISP B for outbound customer traffic, so you prepend your AS toward ISP A to make ISP B's path more likely to be selected by remote networks.
Pitfall: overusing prepend can create unnecessarily long AS paths and complicate path visibility and troubleshooting across multiple peers.
Key Takeaway

Use AS path prepend for outbound de-preferencing. Test effects with advertising-protocol inspections and coordinate with peers when possible.

screens.title: next-hop vs install-nexthop
screens.subtitle: Attribute next-hop and forward-plane install-nexthop contrasted

narration.text: next-hop and install-nexthop both affect where traffic goes, but they operate at different levels. The next-hop action modifies the route attribute so BGP advertisements and route selection reflect a new next-hop; 'next-hop self' is commonly used so the advertising router sets itself as the next-hop for reachability. Install-nexthop is more advanced: it changes the forwarding plane decision for the matched destination by explicitly specifying which next-hop address should be used for forwarding, bypassing a normal routing table lookup for that destination. install-nexthop is useful for service chaining or special forwarding requirements where you must force packets to a particular hop. Because install-nexthop directly influences forwarding, it carries higher operational risk — mistakes can create black holes. A practical contrast: use next-hop self when you need peers to reach the advertiser; use install-nexthop when you need to override forwarding for selected prefixes. Always test install-nexthop in a lab and confirm forwarding behavior with packet-level checks or forwarding table inspection. next-hop vs install-nexthop means next-hop changes route attributes and advertisement; install-nexthop overrides forwarding decisions directly and should be used with caution.. In practical terms, attribute next-hop and forward-plane install-nexthop contrasted. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operational difference
keyIdea.text: next-hop changes route attributes and advertisement; install-nexthop overrides forwarding decisions directly and should be used with caution.

content.html:
Comparison
next-hop (attribute) vs install-nexthop (forwarding)
Understand whether you need to change the route attribute or the actual forwarding decision.
next-hop: modifies the route's next-hop attribute, e.g., next-hop self, to ensure reachability when advertising.
install-nexthop: specifies a forwarding next-hop, bypassing normal routing lookup for that destination.
Examples
# Next-hop
set policy-options policy-statement SET_NEXT_HOP term T1 then next-hop self

# Install-nexthop
set policy-options policy-statement CUSTOM_FORWARDING term T1 then install-nexthop 10.0.0.254
Use next-hop for advertisement reachability; use install-nexthop when you must force forwarding to a specific address for service chaining.
Warning: install-nexthop changes forwarding behavior directly. Test offline and be conservative in production.

screens.title: Comprehensive policy example
screens.subtitle: Walk through a policy that combines actions and flow control

narration.text: Let's step through a comprehensive Junos policy example that combines community tagging, local-preference, next-term, and reject. The example defines communities for no-advertise and an ISP-specific tag, then creates an inbound policy that prefers routes from ISP A by raising local-preference, adding a community, and continuing evaluation. The policy also rejects bogon prefixes and accepts all others. When you inspect this configuration, notice the sequencing: PREFER_ISP_A_ROUTES sets attributes and next-term continues evaluation so a later accept can install the route. The outbound policy uses as-path-prepend and metric to change how the route appears to ISP B, then accepts only intended subnets. Walkthrough steps: read the policy text, map each term to its intended effect, and verify the route attributes with show route protocol bgp detail. Misconfigurations often come from sequencing errors or forgetting accepts. This combined example demonstrates how inbound engineering and outbound advertisement shaping live together in a single policy file; practice reading these blocks to predict runtime behavior before committing them. Comprehensive policy example means trace term-by-term: note attribute changes, flow control, and where final accept or reject happens to predict the route's final state.. In practical terms, walk through a policy that combines actions and flow control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reading policies
keyIdea.text: Trace term-by-term: note attribute changes, flow control, and where final accept or reject happens to predict the route's final state.

content.html:
Lab Walkthrough
Comprehensive policy example
Read and trace the policy to predict how routes are modified and accepted.
policy-options {
    community NO_ADVERTISE members "no-advertise";
    community ISP_A_ROUTES members 65000:100;

    policy-statement INBOUND_ISP_A {
        term PREFER_ISP_A_ROUTES {
            from {
                protocol bgp;
                neighbor 203.0.113.1;
            }
            then {
                local-preference 300;
                community add ISP_A_ROUTES;
                next-term;
            }
        }
        term REJECT_BOGONS {
            from {
                route-filter 10.0.0.0/8 orlonger;
                route-filter 172.16.0.0/12 orlonger;
                route-filter 192.168.0.0/16 orlonger;
            }
            then {
                reject;
            }
        }
        term ACCEPT_ALL_OTHERS {
            then {
                accept;
            }
        }
    }

    policy-statement OUTBOUND_TO_ISP_B {
        term FILTER_INTERNAL_ONLY {
            from {
                protocol direct;
                route-filter 192.168.0.0/16 orlonger;
            }
            then {
                as-path-prepend "65500 65500";
                metric 500;
                community add NO_ADVERTISE;
                accept;
            }
        }
        term REJECT_ALL_OTHERS {
            then { reject; }
        }
    }
}
Trace each term: attributes applied in earlier terms persist unless overwritten, and accept/reject decisions determine final installation and advertisement.

screens.title: Lab activity — create, apply, verify
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: define a community, set local-pref, apply policy, verify

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you through a short lab: create a custom community, build a policy that matches routes from a specific neighbor, set local-preference and add the community, accept those routes, apply the policy to an inbound BGP group, and finally verify the attribute changes. Start by defining a community like CUSTOMER_X_ROUTES with an ASN-tag pair. Next, create a policy-statement with a term that matches neighbor 10.0.0.1 and sets local-preference 150 and community add CUSTOMER_X_ROUTES, then accept. Apply the policy to the BGP group for that neighbor as an import policy. After committing, verify with show route protocol bgp detail for routes learned from 10.0.0.1 and look for the local-preference and community in the output. If the values are not present, re-check term order, match conditions, and whether the policy was applied to the correct group. A common verification step is to use show policy-options to inspect the policy text and show route advertising-protocol to confirm advertisement behavior. This procedure is a compact lab you can run in a two-router or simulated environment to validate your understanding and avoid surprises in production.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Build and verify a policy that sets local-preference and a community, then confirm attributes in route detail output.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Create a routing policy and verify attributes
Follow these steps in a lab environment to prove the concept.
Step 1 — create community
set policy-options community CUSTOMER_X_ROUTES members 65500:500
Step 2 — policy
set policy-options policy-statement INBOUND_TRAFFIC_ENGINEERING term PREFER_CUSTOMER_X from protocol bgp
set policy-options policy-statement INBOUND_TRAFFIC_ENGINEERING term PREFER_CUSTOMER_X from neighbor 10.0.0.1
set policy-options policy-statement INBOUND_TRAFFIC_ENGINEERING term PREFER_CUSTOMER_X then local-preference 150
set policy-options policy-statement INBOUND_TRAFFIC_ENGINEERING term PREFER_CUSTOMER_X then community add CUSTOMER_X_ROUTES
set policy-options policy-statement INBOUND_TRAFFIC_ENGINEERING term PREFER_CUSTOMER_X then accept
Step 3 — apply
set protocols bgp group CUSTOMER_X type external
set protocols bgp group CUSTOMER_X neighbor 10.0.0.1
set protocols bgp group CUSTOMER_X import INBOUND_TRAFFIC_ENGINEERING
commit
Step 4 — verify
show route protocol bgp detail | match "Local preference:|Community:"
# Or filter by prefix learned from 10.0.0.1
If verification fails, inspect show policy-options, check neighbor IPs, term match conditions, and that the policy is applied to the correct BGP group.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Core actions and their operational meaning

narration.text: These compact concept cards summarize the essential facts you should retain. Accept and reject are the final gatekeepers: accept installs a route, reject drops it. Flow control actions — next-term and next-policy — change evaluation order but do not implicitly accept; always ensure an accept exists downstream. Local-preference and as-path-prepend serve different purposes: local-preference steers egress inside your AS and is evaluated early, while as-path-prepend lengthens advertised AS paths to de-prefer routes externally. Communities are flexible tags you can add, set, or delete; remember that set replaces all existing tags whereas add appends. Metric corresponds to MED in BGP and influences how external ASes pick an entry into your AS. Next-hop changes advertisement reachability; install-nexthop overrides forwarding and has higher operational risk. Keep these concepts in mind when you design and verify routing policies.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Actions control acceptance and attributes; sequencing and protocol context determine their real-world effect.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Key Concepts
Accept / Reject
Accept installs a route; reject discards it. Attribute changes do not install by themselves.
next-term / next-policy
Control evaluation flow; ensure a subsequent accept exists or the route will be implicitly rejected.
Local-preference
BGP attribute that biases egress selection inside your AS; higher is preferred.
Summary: use the right action for the protocol, test changes in lab, and verify attributes with route detail commands before deploying widely.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Commands & Cautions
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to keep policies safe and predictable

narration.text: These final three cards remind you of critical operational cautions. First, community add versus set: add appends while set replaces — prefer add to avoid unintentionally stripping upstream tags. Second, metric (MED) is a suggestion to external peers about preferred entry; peers may ignore it, so coordinate with upstreams if you need deterministic results. Third, install-nexthop is powerful but risky: it overrides forwarding decisions and can create black holes if misconfigured. Whenever you use attribute modification or flow control, run verification commands such as show policy-options, show route protocol bgp detail, and show route advertising-protocol bgp to confirm that attribute values and final accept/reject states match your intentions. These checks will help prevent configuration mistakes from causing traffic shifts or outages. Key Concepts — Commands & Cautions means make changes deliberately: prefer additive actions, coordinate with peers for med, and treat install-nexthop as high-impact.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to keep policies safe and predictable. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Final note
keyIdea.text: Make changes deliberately: prefer additive actions, coordinate with peers for MED, and treat install-nexthop as high-impact.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Key Concepts — Commands & Cautions
Community add vs set
add appends, set replaces — use add to preserve upstream tags.
Metric (MED)
Suggests preferred entry to external ASes; peers may ignore or override it.
install-nexthop caution
Overrides forwarding. Validate in lab; avoid accidental black-holing of traffic.
Takeaway

Always verify policy effects with show commands and test in a lab. Sequence actions intentionally and prefer additive, reversible changes when possible.
